claim: Overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system is a hallmark of aging.
source: Overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system is a hallmark of aging.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Aging increases spontaneous and evoked firing responses in sympathetic motor neurons.
source: These approaches showed that aging does impact the intrinsic properties of sympathetic motor neurons, increasing spontaneous and evoked firing responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A reduction of M current is a major contributor to age-related hyperexcitability in sympathetic motor neurons.
source: A reduction of M current emerged as a major contributor to age-related hyperexcitability.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing reduced M current in aged neurons.

claim: With advancing age, the sympathetic nervous system tends to become overactive, evidenced by increased electrical activity in sympathetic nerves.
source: With advancing age, the sympathetic nervous system tends to become overactive, evidenced by increased electrical activity in sympathetic nerves (Wallin et al., 1974; Ito et al., 1986; Narkiewicz et al., 2005; Hart et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sympathetic overactivity in aging leads to heightened release of norepinephrine over organs.
source: This overactivity, observed in humans and animal models, leads to heightened release of norepinephrine over organs (Ziegler et al., 1976; Goldstein et al., 1983a; Goldstein et al., 1983b; Veith et al., 1986; Esler et al., 1995), triggering compensatory processes and cellular deterioration (Hogikyan and Supiano, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Dysregulation of norepinephrine release is associated with age-related hypertension and arrhythmias.
source: For instance, dysregulation of norepinephrine release is associated with age-related hypertension and arrhythmias.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the relationship between norepinephrine and cardiovascular conditions.

claim: Age-associated overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system has been predominantly ascribed to changes in the central system, specifically focusing on the hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei.
source: Age-associated overactivity of the sympathetic nervous system has been predominantly ascribed to changes in the central system, specifically focusing on the hypothalamic and brainstem nuclei.
evidence: This claim summarizes the prevailing view in the field, supported by the citations that follow.

claim: In the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, the activation of glutamatergic neurons through leptin pathways has emerged as a significant contributor to sympathetic overactivity.
source: In the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, the activation of glutamatergic neurons through leptin pathways has emerged as a significant contributor to sympathetic overactivity (Shi et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific research studies.

claim: Glial senescence and subsequent inflammatory mechanisms in brainstem nuclei have been linked to sympathetic nervous system overactivity during aging.
source: At the same time, glial senescence and subsequent inflammatory mechanisms in brainstem nuclei also have been linked to sympathetic nervous system overactivity during aging (Balasubramanian et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Aging impacts the morphology and calcium responses of sympathetic motor neurons.
source: Aging impacts the morphology and calcium responses of sympathetic motor neurons, the peripheral component of the sympathetic reflex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citations and discussion that follow.

claim: Sympathetic innervation to the spleen and lymph nodes reduces with age, while thymus innervation increases.
source: Notably, sympathetic innervation to the spleen and lymph nodes reduces, while thymus innervation increases with age (Madden et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Innervation to vascular smooth muscle changes with age, and the extent and implications of these changes depend on the specific target and neuropeptide content.
source: Similarly, innervation to vascular smooth muscle changes with age, and the extent and implications of these changes depend on the specific target and neuropeptide content (Burnstock, 1990; Andrews and Cowen, 1994; Andrews et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Old sympathetic motor neurons display reduced expression of SERCA pumps.
source: Old sympathetic motor neurons display reduced expression of SERCA pumps, an essential component for calcium transport into the endoplasmic reticulum (Pottorf et al., 2000; Buchholz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sympathetic motor neurons from young adult and old mice are viable in culture.
source: Our first goal was to assess the viability of neurons isolated from young adult and old mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing neurite growth and cell health in culture.

claim: The mean diameter of the cell soma was similar in young (19.7 ± 0.6 μm) and old (19.6 ± 0.6 μm) neurons after 24 and 72 hr in culture.

claim: After 72 hr in culture, the dendritic arborization in old neurons (105 ± 7 μm2) was more extensive compared to that of young neurons (74 ± 5 μm2).

claim: Young neurons had a resting membrane potential (RMP) of –64 ± 1 mV.
source: Young neurons had a resting membrane potential (RMP) of –64 ± 1 mV and very little spontaneous activity, which aligns with the expected behavior of motor neurons that respond to presynaptic commands (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Only 3% of young neurons exhibited spontaneous firing.
source: Only 3% exhibited spontaneous firing (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Middle-aged neurons showed an RMP of –58 ± 1 mV, and 37% of these neurons displayed spontaneous firing.

claim: The mean firing frequency in old neurons (60 ± 20 action potentials [APs]/min) was significantly lower than that observed in middle-aged neurons (177 ± 41 APs/min).

claim: Input resistance was not affected by age in sympathetic motor neurons.

claim: Aging leads to a gradual depolarization of the RMP without significant alteration of the input resistance.

evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data on RMP and input resistance.
